## Interactive: substitution and wages

Move the elasticity of substitution and watch what happens to the wage of each
group. The model is the task-based framework from Lecture 6.

```{ojs}
viewof sigma = Inputs.range([0.2, 4], {value: 1.5, step: 0.1, label: "Elasticity of substitution"})
viewof immig = Inputs.range([0, 0.3], {value: 0.1, step: 0.01, label: "Immigrant share"})

wages = {
  const s = sigma, m = immig;
  const grid = d3.range(0, 0.31, 0.01);
  return grid.map(x => ({
    share: x,
    native: Math.pow(1 - x, -1 / s),
    immigrant: Math.pow(x + 0.01, -1 / s)
  }));
}

Plot.plot({
  marks: [
    Plot.line(wages, {x: "share", y: "native", stroke: "#1E4C7C", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.line(wages, {x: "share", y: "immigrant", stroke: "#C8102E", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.ruleX([immig], {stroke: "#7B4B28", strokeDasharray: "3,3"})
  ],
  x: {label: "Immigrant share of the workforce"},
  y: {label: "Relative wage", domain: [0, 5]},
  style: {backgroundColor: "#EFE3CE", fontFamily: "Jost"},
  height: 300
})
```

Blue is the native wage, crimson the immigrant wage, and the dashed line marks
the share you selected. Raise the elasticity and the two converge: substitutable
workers compete, complementary ones do not.
